title: Supracondylar fracture (anteromedial displacement): median nerve injury
vignette: A 6-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department after falling from a chair onto her outstretched right arm. Physical examination shows swelling of the right elbow and tenderness to palpation over the distal humerus. Radial pulse is slightly diminished in the right upper extremity compared to the left. The patient cannot cooperate with neurologic examination of the right hand due to significant pain. A peripheral intravenous line is placed, and analgesics are administered for pain control. X-ray reveals a supracondylar humeral fracture with anteromedial displacement of the proximal fracture fragment. Which of the following structures is most likely to be injured in this patient?

clues.text: falling from a chair onto her outstretched right arm
clues.note: A fall onto an outstretched arm (hyperextension) is the classic mechanism of a pediatric supracondylar humeral fracture.
A diminished radial pulse signals BRACHIAL ARTERY involvement - which runs with the median nerve in the anteromedial elbow.

clues.text: supracondylar humeral fracture with anteromedial displacement of the proximal fracture fragment
clues.note: ANTEROMEDIAL displacement of the proximal fragment threatens the structures running there - the brachial artery and the MEDIAN nerve (anterolateral displacement would threaten the radial nerve).

whatMatters: A supracondylar humeral fracture with ANTEROMEDIAL displacement of the proximal fragment (plus a diminished radial pulse) injures the structures coursing anteromedially at the elbow: the BRACHIAL ARTERY and the MEDIAN NERVE. Answer C (median nerve). Anterolateral displacement would instead threaten the radial nerve.
strategy: Map the elbow neurovasculature to the displacement direction. Anteromedial = brachial artery + median nerve (diminished radial pulse confirms brachial artery). Anterolateral = radial nerve. Posterior/medial epicondyle = ulnar nerve. So anteromedial displacement -> median nerve (with brachial artery). Reject radial nerve (anterolateral), ulnar nerve (medial epicondyle/flexion injuries), basilic vein (superficial, spared), and biceps tendon (adult distal biceps rupture).

eliminations.label: Basilic vein - superficial, not typically injured
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: a superficial vein over the medial arm/elbow. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: it runs superficially and is not commonly injured in supracondylar fractures (which threaten the deep brachial artery/median nerve). ✅ Correct if: superficial venous injury/venipuncture site.

eliminations.label: Biceps tendon - adult flexed-elbow injury
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: the distal biceps tendon inserting on the radius. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: distal biceps rupture occurs in ADULTS during forceful extension of a flexed, contracting elbow (lifting), not in a pediatric supracondylar fracture. ✅ Correct if: an adult with a sudden 'pop' lifting a heavy object.

eliminations.label: Radial nerve - ANTEROLATERAL displacement (your pick)
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: the radial nerve runs anterior to the LATERAL epicondyle. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: it is threatened by ANTEROLATERAL displacement (causing wrist drop); this fracture is displaced ANTEROMEDIALLY, endangering the median nerve/brachial artery instead. ✅ Correct if: anterolateral displacement (radial nerve, wrist drop).

eliminations.label: Ulnar nerve - medial epicondyle / hyperflexion
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: the ulnar nerve runs POSTERIOR to the medial epicondyle. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: it is injured with medial epicondyle fractures or hyperflexion injuries, not anteromedial displacement of a supracondylar fracture. ✅ Correct if: medial epicondyle fracture (ulnar claw/sensory loss of 5th digit).

reasoning: Fall on an outstretched arm -> supracondylar humeral fracture (hyperextension)
Anteromedial displacement of the proximal fragment threatens the anteromedial structures
The brachial artery (diminished radial pulse) and MEDIAN nerve run anteromedially at the elbow
mechanism: Supracondylar humeral fractures are common pediatric elbow fractures, typically from a hyperextension injury (a fall onto an outstretched arm). At the elbow, the BRACHIAL ARTERY and MEDIAN NERVE run together over the anteromedial aspect (near the medial epicondyle), while the RADIAL nerve lies over the lateral epicondyle and the ULNAR nerve runs posterior to the medial epicondyle. Because the sharp proximal fragment can lacerate or stretch whatever lies in its path, the DIRECTION of displacement predicts the injury: ANTEROMEDIAL displacement (as here) endangers the brachial artery (producing a diminished radial pulse) and the MEDIAN nerve (impairing thumb/finger flexion and sensation over the lateral palm/first three digits), whereas ANTEROLATERAL displacement endangers the RADIAL nerve (wrist drop). Supracondylar fractures therefore carry a real risk of neurovascular compromise and require prompt assessment. The basilic vein is superficial (spared), and distal biceps tendon rupture is an adult injury from forceful elbow flexion - neither fits this pediatric anteromedial supracondylar fracture.

difficulty.label: 🧠 Knowledge
difficulty.text: First Aid Anatomy/MSK > supracondylar humeral fracture: fall on outstretched arm; anteromedial displacement -> brachial artery + median nerve; anterolateral -> radial nerve; ulnar nerve with medial epicondyle/hyperflexion.

difficulty.label: 📖 Comprehension
difficulty.text: Anteromedial displacement + diminished radial pulse = brachial artery + median nerve injury.

difficulty.label: 🔤 Vocab
difficulty.text: Unsure on supracondylar fracture, anteromedial vs anterolateral displacement, or the elbow's nerve/artery relations? Tell me which.

difficulty.label: 🨤 Distractor
difficulty.text: Radial nerve = anterolateral (wrist drop); ulnar nerve = medial epicondyle; basilic vein superficial; biceps tendon = adult injury.

difficulty.label: 🗒️ Other
difficulty.text: Bank: supracondylar fracture anteromedial displacement -> median nerve + brachial artery (↓radial pulse); anterolateral -> radial nerve.

keywords.back: Median nerve + brachial artery injury (↓radial pulse)
Posterior to medial epicondyle; medial epicondyle fracture/hyperflexion
Weak thumb/finger flexion, sensory loss over lateral palm/first 3 digits
Adult; forceful flexion of a loaded elbow

firstAid.detail: MSK: anteromedial displacement -> median nerve + brachial artery.
Anatomy > radial (lateral), ulnar (medial epicondyle), median/brachial artery (anteromedial).
Ortho > assess pulses + nerve function urgently in supracondylar fractures.

memoryHook: The proximal fragment stabs whatever's in front of it: displaced anteroMEDIALLY, it skewers the MEDIAN nerve and brachial artery (pulse drops); anterolaterally would hit the radial nerve.
